# Partner Now, Own the Data: The Only Option That Clears 2027 Without Giving the Asset Away

*Build, buy or partner for condition-based maintenance across 40 critical assets?*

Partner with an engineering firm: it is the only option that meets the January 2027 deadline and keeps the labelled failure history in the operator's hands<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. Building in-house is cheapest at 3.1 million euros but lands six to twelve months late<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>; buying a platform is fastest but leaves 60 percent of failure signals unread and the data asset vendor-bound<sup>[5](source-05-fraunhofer.md)</sup>. The board should approve the partnership by December and hold the partner to a connector handover at month nine.

---

## Context: The Decision Frame

The operator must decide by December 2026 how to stand up condition-based maintenance across 40 critical assets. The decision is a real one: three courses of action are on the table, each already scoped and costed, and the question before the board is not whether to monitor but how. The EU Machinery Regulation applies in full from January 2027 and requires a documented condition-monitoring process for safety-relevant assets; the VDMA puts the average implementation gap at 14 months, which makes late 2025 the last comfortable start and December 2026 the last defensible decision date<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. Three constraints bound the choice. The maintenance team is 60 people in a labour market losing 23 percent of qualified technicians by 2030<sup>[2](source-02-destatis.md)</sup>. The insurers have announced surcharges on unmonitored critical assets from 2027, worth 0.9 million euros over three years to an operator of this size<sup>[3](source-03-handelsblatt.md)</sup>. And the plant produces 47 sensor data formats, so any monitoring approach must eventually read all of them or accept blind spots<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. The three options are assessed below on the same five criteria; nothing in this frame favours one of them yet.

## Tension: The Trade-offs That Matter

Five criteria discriminate between the options, in this order of weight. Time to compliance comes first, because a missed deadline converts into insurance surcharges and a retrofit premium regardless of anything else the option does well<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. Ownership of the data asset comes second: three years of labelled failure history is the thing competitors cannot buy retroactively, and the plants that hold it report 34 percent fewer unplanned stops than those that do not<sup>[5](source-05-fraunhofer.md)</sup>. Three-year cost comes third — real money, but the spread between the options is 1.7 million euros against a compound cost of inaction several times that<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. Dependence on scarce technicians comes fourth, because the sector-wide decline turns every labour-intensive design into a rising cost<sup>[2](source-02-destatis.md)</sup>. Reversibility comes fifth: it matters, but only if the first two criteria are met, since an option that misses the deadline is not one the board can afford to reverse out of. The governing trade-off runs between the first two criteria. The option that clears the deadline most comfortably is the one that gives the asset away, and the option that keeps the asset most cheaply is the one that misses the deadline<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. Every factor on which the options score alike — the 24 lost production hours a year at 180,000 euros each, the compliance obligation itself — is held constant and left out of the comparison<sup>[5](source-05-fraunhofer.md)</sup>.

## Options: The Strategic Alternatives

**Option A — build in-house.** It is an asset-health integration built by the plant's own data team on the plant's own failure history, connector by connector. It delivers full ownership of connectors and history at the lowest three-year cost of the three, 3.1 million euros<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. It fails the first criterion: 18 to 24 months to compliance misses the deadline by six to twelve months and therefore triggers both the insurance surcharge and the retrofit premium of 1.4 million euros against 0.6 million for a planned programme<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. It scores worst on technician dependence, since it leans on the same 60-person team the sector is thinning by 23 percent<sup>[2](source-02-destatis.md)</sup>, and best on reversibility, because nothing is committed until the integration layer reaches production.

**Option B — buy a monitoring platform.** It is a licensed product rolled out plant by plant, with the vendor's connector set and the vendor's schema. It clears the deadline in 9 to 12 months and needs few technicians, which satisfies the first and fourth criteria outright<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. It fails the second: products on the market read 8 to 12 of the plant's 47 formats, so roughly 60 percent of failure signals in the long tail stay unread unless custom connectors are added, and the failure history accrues in the vendor's schema rather than the operator's<sup>[5](source-05-fraunhofer.md)</sup>. Three-year cost is the highest at 4.8 million euros including licences and integration services<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>, and reversibility falls to low after the first year, because the labelled history — the asset the second criterion protects — is by then vendor-bound.

**Option C — partner with an engineering firm.** It is a co-developed integration in which the partner brings the connector library and trains the in-house team while the operator retains the connectors and the history under the co-development terms. It clears the deadline at 12 to 14 months — at the edge, but inside<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. Three-year cost is 4.2 million euros, between the other two<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. Technician dependence is moderate and falls as the team is trained; reversibility is moderate, with the partner replaceable after the connector handover at month nine. On the two criteria that carry the most weight it is the only option that scores on both.

## Choice: The Recommended Path

Choose Option C. It is the only alternative that satisfies the two criteria that carry the most weight at once — it clears the deadline and it keeps the data asset — and it does so at a cost 0.6 million euros below the platform licence<sup>[1](source-01-vdma-regulation.md)</sup>. You accept one trade-off knowingly: 1.1 million euros more than building in-house over three years, which buys twelve months of compliance margin and a connector library the team would otherwise spend those months writing while the surcharge accrued<sup>[4](source-04-vdma-study.md)</sup>. Two conditions protect the choice. Write the month-nine connector handover and the operator's ownership of the failure history into the co-development contract, or the option collapses into Option B by another name. And set one trigger to reopen the decision: if the partner's connector coverage at month six reads fewer than 40 of the 47 formats, the compliance timeline is at risk and the platform becomes the fallback, because clearing the deadline outranks owning the asset when both cannot be had<sup>[5](source-05-fraunhofer.md)</sup>. The uncertainty that matters is the partner's delivery pace, not the evidence, and the trigger is observable at month six. The board does not need more analysis to decide; it needs the contract terms in front of it and a named owner for the month-six coverage reading. Choose C; accept the 1.1 million premium; revisit if coverage stalls at month six.
